title: Episode 26: The Golden Spike and the Great Railroad Race of 1869
description:
On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met to complete the Transcontinental Railroad. Blasting through the granite cliffs of the Sierra Nevada and racing across the Great Plains, thousands of Chinese and Irish laborers achieved one of the greatest engineering feats in human history, culminating in a telegraph wire tied to a silver hammer that broadcast 'DONE' across the globe.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the mid-nineteenth century, a journey across the North American continent was a perilous six-month ordeal. Travelers had to brave deadly cholera across trackless plains or endure a grueling six-month voyage by wooden sailing ship around the treacherous waters of Cape Horn. But in the midst of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signed a daring law to bind the fractured nation with twin ribbons of steel. Two rival railroad empires—the Central Pacific building east from Sacramento, and the Union Pacific building west from Omaha—embarked on an epic, cutthroat race across two thousand miles of untamed desert and solid granite mountains. On May tenth, eighteen sixty-nine, at a remote summit in the Utah desert, a golden spike and a telegraph wire signaled to a waiting world that the continent was finally united. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: LINCOLN'S VISION AND THE PACIFIC RAILWAY ACT
In July eighteen sixty-two, with the Union locked in a desperate, bloody struggle for its survival in the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signed into law the Pacific Railway Act. Lincoln understood that California's immense gold reserves and Pacific ports were vital to the Union's future, yet the Pacific coast was separated from Washington by nearly two thousand miles of impassable mountains and hostile wilderness. The Act commissioned two private corporations to build a transcontinental railroad: the Central Pacific Railroad of California would build eastward from Sacramento across the towering Sierra Nevada, while the Union Pacific Railroad would build westward from the Missouri River at Omaha across the Great Plains. To incentivize speed, Congress offered the companies immense financial bounties: sixteen thousand dollars in government bonds for every mile of track laid on flat plains, thirty-two thousand dollars per mile in the high desert basins, and forty-eight thousand dollars per mile through rugged mountain ranges, alongside millions of acres of public land grants. What began as a national infrastructure project quickly transformed into an intense, hyper-competitive corporate race, as each railroad fought desperately to lay as many miles of track as possible to claim the lion's share of federal cash and land.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CHINESE WALL OF THE SIERRA NEVADA
For the Central Pacific, the race began with what seemed an insurmountable physical barrier: the Sierra Nevada mountains, a colossal granite wall rising over seven thousand feet within just one hundred miles of Sacramento. When white laborers repeatedly abandoned the punishing construction camps to rush off to newly discovered silver strikes in Nevada, Central Pacific construction boss Charles Crocker took a radical, controversial gamble. In eighteen sixty-five, he began hiring thousands of Chinese immigrant workers who had arrived during the Gold Rush. Skeptical supervisors scoffed that the slight Chinese laborers could not handle heavy railroad construction, to which Crocker famously retorted: 'Did they not build the Great Wall of China?' Over twelve thousand Chinese workers became the indispensable backbone of the Central Pacific. Facing brutal winters with forty-foot snowdrifts, the Chinese laborers carved fifteen tunnels through solid granite using only hand drills, sledgehammers, and unstable black powder and nitroglycerin. Suspended hundreds of feet above roaring rivers in wicker baskets woven from river reeds, workers hand-drilled blast holes into sheer vertical cliffs, lit short fuses, and signaled frantically to be pulled up before the dynamite exploded. Hundreds sacrificed their lives to avalanches and blasts, but their astonishing endurance and engineering discipline conquered the Sierra.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE HELL ON WHEELS ROLLING BABYLON ACROSS THE PLAINS
Meanwhile, fifteen hundred miles to the east, the Union Pacific was racing across the flat, boundless expanses of Nebraska and Wyoming. Directed by ruthless Civil War general Grenville Dodge and financed by the notoriously corrupt financier Thomas Durant, the Union Pacific mobilized an army of over ten thousand laborers, consisting predominantly of newly arrived Irish immigrants, Civil War veterans from both Union and Confederate armies, and freed African Americans. Moving with military precision, the track layers became an unstoppable machine. Surveyors rode ahead under cavalry escort, followed by graders who leveled the roadbed, bridge-builders who threw timber trestles across rushing rivers, and finally the iron men who dropped rails onto ties with rhythmic, clockwork precision, laying up to two miles of track every single day. Trailing immediately behind the end of track was a notorious, nomadic shantytown known as 'Hell on Wheels.' Composed of portable canvas tents, rolling saloon wagons, dance halls, and gambling dens, Hell on Wheels was disassembled and moved forward every few weeks as the tracks progressed. It was a violent, whiskey-fueled frontier Babylon where drunken gunfights and knife brawls were nightly occurrences, yet by the dawn of eighteen sixty-nine, the Union Pacific had conquered the Rocky Mountains and was racing down into the Great Salt Lake Basin.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PARALLEL GRADES AND THE BITTER UTAH RIVALRY
As the two rail lines converged in northern Utah in early eighteen sixty-nine, the rivalry reached a fever pitch of competitive frenzy. Because Congress had never designated an exact meeting point where the two railroads should connect, both corporations realized that every additional mile of track laid meant thousands more dollars in government subsidies and square miles of land grants. Instead of joining their tracks when they drew near, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific construction crews began grading rail beds parallel to each other. For more than two hundred miles across the Utah desert, rival construction crews worked side by side, sometimes within shouting distance of only a few hundred feet. Irish graders for the Union Pacific and Chinese graders for the Central Pacific glared across the desert sands, exchanging insults that soon escalated into sabotage and violence. Union Pacific crews routinely set off unannounced heavy dynamite blasts right next to Central Pacific grades, showering Chinese laborers with boulders. The Chinese workers retaliated by secretly placing a subterranean powder charge beneath the Union Pacific roadbed, blowing dozens of feet of their rival's grade into the air. Finally, alarmed by the wasteful expenditure of public funds and mounting violence, Congress intervened in April eighteen sixty-nine, ordering the heads of both lines to halt the madness and officially designating Promontory Summit as the permanent junction.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TEN-MILE DAY IN THE PROMONTORY DESERT
Even with the meeting point settled, the competitive fire between the two rail empires burned hotter than ever. Union Pacific vice president Thomas Durant boasted that his Irish crews had set an unbeatable record by laying seven miles of track in a single day. Central Pacific construction boss Charles Crocker immediately responded with a wager of ten thousand dollars—a staggering fortune at the time—betting that his crews could lay ten miles in a single twenty-four-hour period. On April twenty-eighth, eighteen sixty-nine, Crocker orchestrated an astonishing exhibition of human speed and organization. Beginning at sunrise, an elite crew of eight Irish track layers—supported by thousands of Chinese laborers who hauled wooden ties, scattered ballast, and drove iron spikes—swarmed over the desert roadbed. Working in blistering heat with rhythmic, clockwork precision, the men advanced at the pace of a walking horse. By midday, they had laid six miles of track. After a quick break for lunch, they resumed their furious pace, hammering ties until the sun sank behind the desert mountains. When the final rail was fastened, Crocker's men had laid ten miles and fifty-six feet of iron track in less than twelve hours. The eight iron men had lifted more than two million pounds of steel rails, driving over fifty-five thousand spikes—a world record in heavy manual construction that has never been broken to this day.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SILVER HAMMER AND THE GOLDEN SPIKE
On Monday, May tenth, eighteen sixty-nine, Promontory Summit was crowded with hundreds of rail workers, soldiers, dignitaries, and newspaper reporters for the historic joining of the rails. Two steam locomotives—the Central Pacific's wood-burning Jupiter, painted in brilliant scarlet and blue, and the Union Pacific's coal-burning locomotive Number One Hundred and Nineteen—crept forward until their cowcatchers touched, surrounded by cheering crowds. To commemorate the moment, California financier David Hewes had commissioned a ceremonial seven-inch golden spike cast from pure California gold, inscribed with the words: 'May God continue the unity of our Country as this Railroad unites the two great Oceans of the world.' Nevada contributed a silver spike, and Arizona offered an alloy of gold, silver, and iron. In an unprecedented feat of nineteenth-century technology, the Western Union telegraph wire was attached directly to the ceremonial silver hammer and the golden spike. When Central Pacific President Leland Stanford swung the maul to drive the spike into the ceremonial laurel tie, the electrical impulse flashed across thousands of miles of telegraph wire simultaneously to every city in the nation, flashing the single word: 'DONE.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE TRANSFORMED CONTINENT AND THE IRON LEGACY
The driving of the Golden Spike triggered euphoric nationwide celebrations. In New York City, a hundred naval cannons fired in the harbor, and Trinity Church choir sang the Te Deum; in Philadelphia, the Liberty Bell was rung; in Chicago, a seven-mile parade of citizens flooded the avenues, and in San Francisco, fireworks illuminated the bay. The Transcontinental Railroad fundamentally revolutionized world geography and commerce. A journey across the North American continent that previously required six grueling, dangerous months and cost thousands of dollars could now be completed in just seven days for less than one hundred dollars in a comfortable Pullman sleeper car. Goods, mail, and immigrants poured across the continent, transforming the American interior from a remote frontier into the agricultural and industrial engine of the modern world. Today, the Golden Spike National Historical Park at Promontory preserves the historic summit, where replica steam engines still hiss steam and recreate the historic handshake of iron. It remains an enduring monument to human ambition, engineering genius, and the diverse hands that stitched a continent into a single nation.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The driving of the Golden Spike was more than a triumph of steam and iron; it was the birth of modern America, proving that no mountain was too high and no wilderness too vast for human perseverance. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday for the strange cricket invasion that tested the pioneers of Utah. Until then, stay curious.
